https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: Nearly two centuries after scientists first isolated one of the most chemically complicated substances produced by plants, researchers are uncovering a new way to explore the medicinal possibilities hidden inside two famously poisonous flowers. Wolfsbane and larkspur may be capable of causing severe nerve damage and paralysis in extremely small doses, yet the same plants produce extraordinary molecules that could eventually inspire treatments for pain, malaria, cancer and other applications. A new study from scientists at Michigan State University and the Czech Academy of Sciences has identified six enzymes involved in producing a complex compound called atisinium, offering researchers a potential biological route for studying rare plant chemicals on a larger scale.The discovery highlights a remarkable paradox in natural medicine: substances capable of harming the human body can also provide clues for developing useful therapies. Plants have spent millions of years evolving sophisticated chemical defenses against predators, disease and environmental threats. Humans have repeatedly learned how to study those molecules and, in some cases, turn their unusual biological properties into medicines or other valuable products. Caffeine, menthol, capsaicin and vanillin are familiar examples of plant-derived or plant-inspired chemistry, while numerous modern medicines have roots in compounds first discovered in nature, according to Science Daily.Plant Chemicals ResearchThe latest research focuses on diterpenoid alkaloids, a family of plant chemicals found in species including larkspur and wolfsbane. These molecules are particularly intriguing because their structures are exceptionally complicated. Scientists have known about some of them for generations, but understanding exactly how plants assemble such elaborate chemicals has remained a difficult biological puzzle. Aconitine, one of the best-known members of the family, was isolated nearly 200 years ago, yet researchers have still not successfully synthesized it in a laboratory, according to the research summary.132830883That long-standing challenge is what makes the new work significant. Instead of trying to manufacture the final molecule through conventional chemical synthesis alone, the researchers investigated how the plants themselves build these substances. Their approach was similar to tracing an intricate biological production line. The team studied several species of wolfsbane and larkspur and examined thousands of genes to identify which ones became active in particular tissues at particular stages. By following these molecular clues, the scientists were able to identify genes responsible for key steps in the production process.The international collaboration brought together researchers who had been studying the same difficult family of compounds from different perspectives. Scientists from Michigan State University worked alongside researchers at the Czech Academy of Sciences to examine the chemistry of both larkspur and wolfsbane, also known as monkshood. Their collaboration demonstrates how modern plant science increasingly combines genetics, biochemistry and biotechnology to solve questions that have resisted conventional approaches for decades.Tobacco PlantsOne of the most striking achievements came when the researchers transferred genetic instructions from the poisonous plants into tobacco plants. The modified tobacco plants acted as living biological factories, allowing the scientists to test whether the selected genes could recreate the chemical pathway. The experiment successfully produced the pathway needed to assemble atisinium, with six different enzymes working together to create the complicated compound.The researchers also discovered something unexpected about the process. The enzymes did more than simply reshape the developing molecule. They enabled the addition of nitrogen, an essential component that the team had not initially expected to find incorporated in this part of the pathway. Such discoveries can help scientists understand how plants create unusual chemical structures and potentially identify additional steps in the larger biosynthetic network.Why does recreating a plant's chemistry matter? One major reason is supply. Plants generally produce specialized metabolites in very small quantities and often do so slowly. If scientists want to investigate a rare molecule for possible medical applications, obtaining enough material can become a major obstacle. Understanding the genetic instructions behind production could allow researchers to transfer those instructions into engineered organisms or plant systems that produce larger quantities under controlled conditions.Poisonous PlantsThis approach could eventually provide a more sustainable route to studying natural compounds. Rather than relying entirely on harvesting large quantities of slow-growing or poisonous plants, researchers could potentially use biological production systems to generate molecules for laboratory testing. The current study does not mean that a new drug has been discovered or that atisinium is ready for use in patients. It represents an early scientific step toward understanding and potentially harnessing a complicated family of natural products.The possible medical applications are particularly intriguing because diterpenoid alkaloids have biological activities that may be useful under carefully controlled conditions. Researchers are interested in this broader family because its members could provide starting points for investigating treatments related to pain, malaria and cancer, among other potential applications. But their toxicity is also a major reason why these compounds must be studied cautiously. A naturally occurring substance is not automatically safe simply because it comes from a plant.The research therefore illustrates an important principle of drug discovery: nature does not necessarily provide finished medicines. Instead, it provides chemical structures and biological mechanisms that scientists can investigate, modify and test. A molecule that is too toxic or difficult to produce in its natural form might nevertheless reveal a useful biological pathway or inspire a safer compound in the future.What Happened in 200 years ago?There is also a broader lesson in the history of aconitine. Nearly 200 years after its isolation, scientists are still learning how plants construct members of this chemically challenging family. Modern genetic tools have opened doors that were unavailable to earlier generations of researchers. What once looked like an impenetrable chemical mystery can now be approached by tracking individual genes and enzymes and reconstructing biological pathways in another organism.The study of wolfsbane and larkspur shows why some of the most promising scientific discoveries can emerge from unexpected places. Two flowers known for their danger contain molecular machinery that may help scientists explore future medicines. The immediate breakthrough is not a new treatment but a better understanding of how nature builds extraordinary chemicals.For researchers, that knowledge could become a foundation for future experiments aimed at producing rare molecules more efficiently and sustainably. For medicine, it offers another reminder that the natural world remains an enormous source of chemical possibilities. And for the history of science, it is striking to see a chemical family first explored nearly two centuries ago entering a new era through genetic engineering and plant biotechnology. The poisonous flowers may be dangerous in nature, but their chemistry could provide scientists with valuable tools for discovering what comes next.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Queen Camilla reflects on the period that followed King Charles’s cancer diagnosis in video celebrating 30 years of the charity Maggie’s, of which she is the president. Photograph: @RoyalFamily/Buckingham Palace/PA View image in fullscreen Queen Camilla reflects on the period that followed King Charles’s cancer diagnosis in video celebrating 30 years of the charity Maggie’s, of which she is the president. Photograph: @RoyalFamily/Buckingham Palace/PA Queen Camilla Camilla found it ‘difficult’ keeping king’s cancer diagnosis private before announcement In video celebrating Maggie’s cancer charity, queen recalls ‘longing to let it out’ on visit to centre in 2024 Caroline Davies Wed 19 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 02.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The queen has spoken for the first time of how difficult she found it to keep King Charles’s cancer a secret before it was announced publicly. Camilla found herself “longing to let it out” during an official visit to a Maggie’s cancer support centre in 2024 , after Charles had received his diagnosis but before the news was released. Speaking in a short film, released on the royal family and Maggie’s YouTube channels on Wednesday, to mark the charity’s 30th anniversary, Camilla said she “almost said something” but knew she couldn’t when, as Maggie’s president, she launched its new centre at the Royal Free hospital in London on 31 January 2024. Maggie’s provides free emotional and practical support to cancer patients and their loved-ones at 27 drop-in centres positioned near NHS hospitals across the UK. At the time of Camilla’s visit, Charles was recovering from treatment for an enlarged prostate but, as the film reveals, had already been diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer, which was eventually announced by Buckingham Palace five days later on 5 February. “I remember coming to see a Maggie’s just after the king being diagnosed. Nobody could say anything at the time. That was quite difficult,” she told Maggie’s chief executive, Dame Laura Lee, who was filmed in conversation with Camilla at Clarence House. “I almost said something but, you know, I felt that it wasn’t the time to say. “[I] looked at everybody who was suffering and all the relations and I think it made me realise even more how important these places were.” View image in fullscreen Camilla meets volunteers and visitors at the Maggie’s centre near London’s Royal Free hospital. Photograph: Paul Grover/Daily Telegraph/PA She told Lee: “I was just longing to let it out but obviously I couldn’t.” Talking to visitors at the centre during the engagement, she said she was “almost questioning them”, but she did not “want to pry too deeply”. “But normally when I went in, I was just talking to them, but I don’t know, I felt it was much more deep,” she said. Charles returned to public-facing engagements in April 2024 , less than three months after his treatment began. Speaking of his refusal to slow down, Camilla said: “Look at my husband. Nothing stopped him. He just said, ‘This is my way. I’m going to cope with it.’” She added: “It had never really come back to roost at home, and suddenly your husband is diagnosed, and you think ‘Goodness I’ve been talking to all these people and now I’m the one with some relation, who’s got to help to look after my poor husband and try and understand it all.’” Camilla released the seven-minute film to highlight the vital support Maggie’s offers cancer patients, and to promote the services they provide for relatives and especially to men who may be more reluctant to seek help. She called on every hospital to have a Maggie’s centre. Maggie’s has 27 centres across the UK, built in the grounds of major NHS cancer hospitals, and supports hundreds of thousands of people each year. The organisation offers care for people affected by cancer, including free psychological, emotional and practical support, with no appointments necessary for the drop-in sessions. [GENYA SAVILOV/AFP/GETTY IMAGES/TNS] Genya Savilov Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Russia plans to launch “hybrid-style” drone and missile strikes against nations supporting Ukraine, including NATO-member Poland, as the war enters its most crucial phase. The Kremlin’s main goal now, as supported by evidence gathered by intelligence services, is to destroy Ukraine’s economy and logistics and weaken NATO’s resolve by attacks on its member states, Tusk said in parliament on Thursday. This is the “most likely scenario,” the premier told lawmakers ahead of his planned visit to Ukraine on Friday. Poland, as a key transit route for aid to Ukraine, has suffered a spate of suspicious incidents, with multiple cyberattacks on public utilities like water, energy infrastructure and hospitals, and damage to the rail line between Warsaw and the Ukrainian border attributed to Russian sabotage. A Russian missile crashed in eastern Poland in late July. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles may fly into the territory of one or more NATO countries on the eastern flank, even cause destruction,” Tusk said. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to think about any response from NATO.” The comments were made hours before Tusk met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Moscow has intensified attacks against Ukraine, including at targets close to the Polish border, while NATO jets shot down a drone of Russian origin over Lithuania earlier this week. Tusk’s warnings were echoed by Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, who said on Thursday that the security situation had never been “so serious and so tense.” He stressed that Slovakia takes its NATO commitments seriously, but that he’d do everything in his power to avoid his country being dragged into a conflict. Fico’s position has long diverged from the NATO mainstream, as he doesn’t regard Russia as a security threat and instead advocates rapprochement with Moscow. He warned of the consequences of invoking NATO’s Article 5, which requires members to defend each other from attack, in the event of a direct conflict between NATO and Russia. “Can anyone imagine that we’re told to prepare 5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers? And they’ll go to fight somewhere, we don’t even know with whom, why or for what?” Fico said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a fellow critic of the European mainstream, made similar remarks. “The path the world is on leads straight to the gates of hell. It is leading us to WWIII,” he said at an address to the IISS Prague Defense Summit. French President Emmanuel Macron said he’ll meet with government and party leaders, along with military and security officials, on Friday to address a “rapidly worsening” situation concerning security and energy supplies amid conflicts including Ukraine and the Middle East. Kyiv and its western allies are bracing themselves for what’s likely to be the most difficult winter since the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion four and a half years ago. Tusk said he will discuss with Zelenskyy possible cooperation through the so-called ”anti-ballistic coalition” as well as the situation around Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. “Sustained, very frequent and intense attacks are expected on six major Ukrainian cities, including the destruction of warehouses, all types of products essential for the country’s defense, and, as we have witnessed very strongly in recent weeks, the railway infrastructure,” the prime minister said. According to information Poland has received about U.S.-Russia consultations, the Kremlin isn’t ready for “any serious talks about a ceasefire, not to mention peace without — de-facto — Ukraine’s capitulation,” Tusk said. “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine,” the prime minister said about Russia. — With assistance from Wojciech Moskwa, Daniel Hornak and Michal Kubala. https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text: Patrick Stewart, who has died aged 86, played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Treak: the Next Generation and Charles Xavier in X-Men. Photograph: Philip Cheung/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Patrick Stewart, who has died aged 86, played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Treak: the Next Generation and Charles Xavier in X-Men. Photograph: Philip Cheung/The Guardian Patrick Stewart Patrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86 Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’ Patrick Stewart – a life in pictures Patrick Stewart brought gravitas and complexity to the screen, from Star Trek to X-Men Adrian Horton and Benjamin Lee Thu 29 Oct 2026 17.02 EDT First published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, has died. He was 86. The Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men star died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, said Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, to the Hollywood Reporter . Patrick Stewart – a life in pictures Read more “He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” she wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.” With his authoritative baritone voice and commanding visage, Stewart was already a staple of the British stage by the late 1980s when, at 47, he was cast as a graying Capt Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: the Next Generation, the first live-action spin-off of the groundbreaking 1960s TV series. Over seven seasons onboard the Starship Enterprise, Stewart’s even-keeled performance and steely directives – “engage!” and “make it so” – turned him into a global star. View image in fullscreen Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1990. Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty Images Stewart reprised his role in four feature film spin-offs – Star Trek Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998) and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002) – as well as the TV series Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 until 2023. His longtime friend, fellow Shakespearean actor and X-Men co-star Ian McKellen called him “the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic”. “Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end,” he wrote on social media . “You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.” Harriet Walter, who knew Stewart for more than 40 years and acted opposite him on stage in Antony and Cleopatra at the RSC in 2006 , told BBC Newsnight that the world is “going to be very poor” without him. “I can’t really imagine a world without him,” she said. “It’s like a huge giant tree has fallen in the forest. I’ve never heard a bad word against him.” Fellow Star Trek actor William Shatner paid tribute on social media. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did,” he wrote . “Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.” ‘On stage, I could escape’: Sir Patrick Stewart on childhood trauma and acting success Read more George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original series, also wrote about Stewart on Bluesky. “He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity,” he posted . “Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.” His other most well-known role was playing Prof Charles Xavier in the X-Men series. The actor had found work hard to obtain after feeling typecast as a result of his Star Trek role but had been intrigued by working with director Bryan Singer for 2000’s X-Men. He went on to play the role in seven films and will be seen reprising the role in this December’s Avengers: Doomsday. View image in fullscreen Patrick Stewart as Charles Xavier in X-Men 2. Photograph: Marvel/Allstar His X-Men co-star Hugh Jackman shared on Instagram: “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.” Marvel chief Kevin Feige has paid tribute in a statement calling him “brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas … Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.” Stewart’s other film roles included the gay comedy Jeffrey, romantic thriller Conspiracy Theory, violent horror Green Room and voice roles in Ted, Gnomeo & Juliet and, most recently, The Sheep Detectives. View image in fullscreen Patrick Stewart and Ian Holm on stage in The Iceman Cometh. Photograph: Donald Cooper/Alamy Born on 13 July 1940 in the small industrial village of Mirfield, England, Stewart was the youngest of three sons born to Alfred Stewart, a British military veteran turned semiskilled laborer, and Gladys Stewart, a weaver at a textile factory. His childhood, in a small house with no running hot water, was marred by alcoholism and domestic violence, a situation he later described, in an article for the Guardian from 2009, as “barely tolerable”. He found respite in acting, first in school – he was 12 when an English teacher assigned him the part of Shylock in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice – and then local drama groups. “I managed to find my own refuge in acting,” he wrote. “The stage was a far safer place for me than anything I had to live through at home – it offered escape. I could be someone else, in another place, in another time.” After graduating from secondary school at 15, he worked as a local reporter and furniture salesman before a local arts council provided the funding to attend the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theater School, where he enrolled in 1957, at 17. Having shed his Yorkshire accent, he took his first professional theater role two years later, and in 1966 joined the Royal Shakespeare Company. During his 16 years with the company, Stewart developed a reputation as one of the finest thespians of his era and a representative of Shakespeare to new audiences; it was while conducting master classes on Shakespeare in LA, at the invitation of a friend, that he first caught the eye of a TV casting director for Star Trek. Stewart made his Broadway debut in 1971 in Peter Brook’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and appeared again 20 years later in a solo production of A Christmas Carol. The holiday season show, which he revived in 1992, 1994 and 2001, received a Drama Desk award. View image in fullscreen David Tennant as Hamlet and Patrick Stewart as Claudius, in a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Hamlet. Photograph: Robbie Jack/Corbis/Getty Images Over the course of his career, Stewart embodied many of Shakespeare’s signature roles, including Macbeth, Othello, Prospero, Shylock and Mark Antony. He was the recipient of two Laurence Olivier awards – in 1979, for Antony and Cleopatra, and in 2009 for Hamlet – as well as a Grammy in 1996 for a spoken word children’s album Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf. He was also nominated for a Tony and four Emmys. His final major stage role was in 2016, when he appeared as Hirst in Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land at London’s Wyndham Theatre. In 2023, he released his memoir called Making It So. Stewart was a vocal fan of Huddersfield Town FC since he was a child and was seen cheering them on most recently in 2024. In a Facebook post from the official team, he was called “a titan of his craft and a legend and hero to millions worldwide”. Stewart was married three times: to theater choreographer Sheila Falconer, from 1966 until 1990 and with whom he had two children, fellow actors Daniel and Sophie; to Star Trek producer Wendy Neuss from 2000 until 2003; and to jazz musician Sunny Ozell from 2013 until his death. His friend and occasional collaborator Ian McKellen, with whom Stewart starred in two Broadway productions in 2013, officiated his final wedding after a rehearsal. “I think I’ve been in denial about my life for a very long time,” he said to the Guardian in a 2023 interview . “I never really took on board how successful I had become. Even today I sometimes think, ‘You’re a lucky son of a bitch, Patrick,’ when something unexpected or good happens to me.” Explore more on these topics Patrick Stewart Star Trek Television US television news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world
